docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Inline Agents turns "run this workflow" instructions in an Obsidian note into a button. Click it, and it fires Claude Code or OpenCode at the note, in a live terminal right underneath — or, if you'd rather not watch it work, quietly in the background with the result dropped straight into the note when it's done.

Or hand the prompt to an agent you already run elsewhere. With target: <name>, the button sends its prompt over HTTP to an agent runtime — OpenClaw, Hermes Agent, or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint — and the work carries on there. See Agent Runtimes.

Built to replace plain-text "Run features/learning-artefacts/teacher-artefact-leveller.md" instructions scattered across a note system with something clickable.

Drop a fenced code block with the agent-button language tag anywhere in a note:

```agent-button
text: Draft this week's report
prompt: Draft a weekly report for {{file.basename}}, using the notes tagged #weekly-log from the last 7 days.
agent: ClaudeCode
model: myMainModel
showTerminal: true
completion: manual
```

That's it — every field except text and prompt is optional. Click the button and you get a real terminal, right in the note:

docs.title: What you could use it for
docs.text:
• A "Run sufficiency check" button under every artefact note, instead of remembering the exact command.
  • A background summarizer that appends its findings to the bottom of a daily note and never opens a terminal you have to watch.
  • Different buttons on the same note routed to different agents or different models — a fast local model for a quick pass, a bigger one for the real thing.
  • A "Hand to my agent" button that sends the note to OpenClaw or Hermes Agent, so the work runs with that agent's own memory and tools while you carry on in Obsidian.
  • Prompts that pull real context from the note — frontmatter status, tags, the vault name — instead of static text you have to edit by hand every time.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Each agent-button code block is its own self-contained widget, rendered via Obsidian's own registerMarkdownCodeBlockProcessor. Clicking the button:

  1. Renders the prompt: template against a snapshot of the note (file path, frontmatter, tags, the vault, today's date — see Context and Templating).
  2. Resolves which agent binary to run and, if a model: line is set, which model to pass it — see Agents and Models.
  3. Spawns the CLI behind a real PTY and feeds its output into a live xterm.js terminal in an accordion under the button — a real terminal, not a plain text log. Type into it exactly like a normal terminal whenever the agent isn't auto-approving.
  4. Once the process exits (or, in responseEnd completion mode, once the agent finishes its reply), the button returns to idle — and if agentOutput: file is set, the result is written straight into the note:

A button with target: <name> skips steps 2–4: the rendered prompt goes to the named agent runtime over HTTP, the button shows "Sent to <name>", and you read the reply on the runtime.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text:
• New to the plugin? Start with Installation and Your First Button.
  • Want the full agent-button spec? See All Fields.
  • Want to send a button's prompt to OpenClaw or Hermes Agent? See Agent Runtimes.
  • Want prompts that adapt to the note they're in? See Context and Templating.
  • Something not behaving as expected? Check the FAQ and Troubleshooting.

docs.title: Changelog
docs.text: The full, authoritative changelog is the project's GitHub Releases page — every release ships main.js, manifest.json, and styles.css as downloadable assets alongside its notes.
• Shorter plugin description in manifest.json (230 characters), to fit the community store's 250-character limit. No code changes.

• Buttons can now send their prompt to an HTTP agent runtime instead of the inline terminal — target: <name> hands off to a configured runtime (an OpenClaw hook, or any OpenAI-compatible chat endpoint, e.g. Hermes Agent) and opens the resulting thread. New open: and agentId: button fields, a new Agent runtimes section in Settings (name, kind, base URL, token, agent/model, thread-URL template, "Test connection"), and a per-device token stored in Obsidian's own secret storage, never in data.json. See Agent Runtimes.
• Fixed a TDZ (temporal dead zone) crash in runCommand() that permanently blocked OpenCode's model refresh.

• prompt: templates: {{ path.to.value }} context lookups (file, vault, date) and an opt-in {{= expression }} mini expression language, replacing the old single {{this file}} placeholder. See Context and Templating.

• Per-provider Model mappings in Settings — a model: field on agent-button blocks, a live model dropdown for OpenCode, a curated static list for Claude Code, and a green/red connection-status dot per provider. See Model Mappings.
• agent-button blocks can set agent: ClaudeCode / agent: OpenCode to override the plugin-wide default per button. The plugin-wide setting was relabeled Default Agent for clarity.

docs.title: 0.1.0 – 0.1.3
docs.text:
• Initial release: the agent-button code block, live PTY-backed terminal, completion: manual / responseEnd, agentOutput: file capture, and the settings tab.

See each release's own notes on GitHub for the full detail behind these.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: Copy-pasteable agent-button blocks for common setups. Adjust prompt:, agent:, and model: to match your own vault and Settings.

docs.title: A sufficiency-check workflow, output written into the note
docs.text:
```agent-button
text: Run Sufficiency Check
prompt: Run features/learning-artefacts/teacher-artefact-sufficiency-check.md on {{file.path}}
autoApprove: true
agent: ClaudeCode
agentOutput: file
append: belowButton
showTerminal: false
completion: responseEnd
```

docs.title: A prompt that branches on frontmatter status
docs.text:
Requires Allow JavaScript expressions in prompts turned on (see Context and Templating):

```agent-button
text: Draft or review
prompt: {{= file.frontmatter.status === "draft" ? "Finish drafting " + file.basename : "Review " + file.basename }}
agent: ClaudeCode
```

docs.title: A fast local pass with a mapped Ollama model
docs.text:
Assumes an OpenCode ollama provider is configured (see opencode.ai/docs/providers) and a mapping named local-fast is set up in Settings pointing at it — see Model Mappings:

```agent-button
text: Quick local summary
prompt: Summarize the open action items in {{file.path}} as a short bulleted list.
agent: OpenCode
model: local-fast
showTerminal: true
completion: manual
```

docs.title: A literal model string, no mapping configured
docs.text:
Useful for a one-off test before you've set up a mapping — pastes straight from a dropdown's copy button:

```agent-button
text: Try a specific model
prompt: Summarize {{file.basename}}.
agent: OpenCode
model: ollama/qwen3.8:27b-mlx
showTerminal: true
completion: manual
```

docs.title: An auto-approved background run, result appended to the note
docs.text:
```agent-button
text: File a follow-up (background)
prompt: Check {{file.path}} for anything marked TODO and list them.
agent: ClaudeCode
autoApprove: true
agentOutput: file
append: belowButton
showTerminal: false
completion: responseEnd
```

Result, once the underlying session eventually closes:

docs.title: Multiple buttons, different agents, on the same note
docs.text:
Nothing stops different buttons on the same note from routing to different agents or models — a fast pass and a thorough pass side by side:

```agent-button
text: Draft this week's report
prompt: Draft a weekly report for {{file.basename}}, using the notes tagged #weekly-log from the last 7 days.
agent: ClaudeCode
model: myMainModel
showTerminal: true
completion: manual
```

```agent-button
text: Summarize with OpenCode
prompt: Summarize the open action items in {{file.path}} as a short bulleted list.
agent: OpenCode
showTerminal: true
completion: manual
```

docs.title: Hand a button off to an OpenClaw hook
docs.text:
Requires an OpenClaw instance at http://127.0.0.1:18789 with its hook enabled, allowRequestSessionKey: true and "inline:" allowed in allowedSessionKeyPrefixes — see Agent Runtimes — and a runtime named openclaw configured in Settings:

```agent-button
text: Run weekly review
prompt: Run the weekly review on {{file.path}}
target: openclaw
```

Clicking it shows "Sending to openclaw…", then "Sent to openclaw ↗" — the thread keeps running on OpenClaw even after the note or Obsidian closes.

docs.title: Hand a button off to a Hermes Agent (OpenAI-compatible chat)
docs.text:
Requires a Hermes Agent API server at http://127.0.0.1:8642/v1 and a runtime named hermes (kind OpenAI-compatible chat) configured in Settings — see Agent Runtimes:

```agent-button
text: Summarize today's notes
prompt: Summarize today's journal entries into three bullet points.
target: hermes
open: false
```

open: false sends the prompt without opening anything — the button still shows "Sent to hermes" (Hermes has no thread link yet), and the run lasts only as long as Obsidian stays open.

docs.title: A provider's status dot is red
docs.text:
The configured binary doesn't resolve or doesn't run (<bin> --version failed). Check:

  • Is the CLI actually installed? A red dot most commonly just means it isn't.
  • Is the binary path in Settings correct, or is it a bare command name that isn't on the PATH Obsidian sees? GUI apps on macOS don't always inherit your shell's PATH — see Claude Code and OpenCode.
  • The dot only checks that the binary runs — it doesn't check login/auth. A green dot with a failing button usually means an auth problem, not a plugin problem; check the CLI's own login state directly (e.g. claude doctor).

docs.title: Claude Code fails with "--dangerously-skip-permissions cannot be used with root/sudo privileges"
docs.text: Claude Code's own CLI refuses that flag when the process runs as root — this happens if Obsidian itself is running as root (common in some container setups). It's a Claude Code safety restriction, not something the plugin can route around. Either run Obsidian as a non-root user, or turn off auto-approve for that button and approve tool calls manually in the terminal.

docs.title: A button's model: value doesn't seem to do anything
docs.text: Check that the mapping name you typed matches one configured under the agent that button actually resolves to — mappings are scoped per provider, so a Claude Code mapping named quick isn't visible to a button using agent: OpenCode. If nothing matches, the value is passed straight through as a literal model string, which most CLIs reject as unknown if it isn't a real model ID — see Model Mappings.

docs.title: A {{= }} expression does nothing / errors
docs.text: {{= }} expressions are off by default. Turn on Allow JavaScript expressions in prompts in Settings — see Context and Templating. While off, a button whose prompt contains {{= }} writes a clear error to the terminal instead of running.

docs.title: A {{ }} lookup shows up literally in the sent prompt instead of being replaced
docs.text: That means the root name wasn't recognized (a typo like {{flie.basename}}) — this is deliberate, so the mistake stays visible rather than silently vanishing. Check the spelling against the Context Reference. A missing value under a real root (e.g. no frontmatter status field) renders as an empty string instead, which looks different from this case.

docs.title: A target: runtime button fell back to the terminal instead of sending
docs.text:
Every fallback shows a notice naming the reason, then runs the button in the terminal exactly as if target: had been terminal all along — see Agent Runtimes for the full detail. Quick reference:

Notice Fix Unknown target "<name>" — running the default target instead. The target: name doesn't match any configured runtime — check Agent runtimes in Settings, or fix the typo in the button. <name> isn't reachable, running here The runtime's HTTP server isn't running, or isn't reachable at its configured base URL — start/check it there, outside Obsidian. token rejected The token Settings has for this runtime, on this device, was rejected (401/403) — re-enter the correct one. Token not set on this device for "<name>". No token is stored for this runtime on this device — settings synced from elsewhere carry the runtime's configuration but never its token; enter it in Settings here. OpenClaw rejected the session key: enable allowRequestSessionKey and allow the inline: prefix On the OpenClaw side, turn on allowRequestSessionKey and add "inline:" to allowedSessionKeyPrefixes.

docs.title: The plugin needs python3 — is that a problem?
docs.text:
The terminal is allocated via python3 -c "import pty,sys; pty.spawn(sys.argv[1:])" rather than a native node-pty build, specifically to avoid needing a fresh native prebuild every time Obsidian's bundled Electron version changes. This needs a python3 at one of a few standard locations, or on PATH — true on basically any Mac or Linux environment already. If it's genuinely missing, install Python 3 for your OS and it'll be picked up.

An earlier attempt used BSD script -q /dev/null, which is broken specifically when Obsidian spawns it (script: tcgetattr/ioctl: Operation not supported on socket) — this is why python3 is used instead, not script.

docs.title: Other things worth knowing
docs.text:
• Binary path resolution is best-effort, not exhaustive — an unusual install location may need to be set explicitly in Settings.
  • agentOutput: file and completion: responseEnd are both heuristic, pattern-matching the rendered terminal against text Claude Code has been observed to print — a CLI update or unusual output can occasionally misclassify a run. See Completion Modes and Captured File Output.
  • Closing the note kills a manual-mode run. Each button's process is tied to its block's lifetime — navigating away sends the child process SIGINT. A responseEnd run does outlive the button going idle, but not the note being closed.
  • No live terminal resize signal to the child — a long run in a pane you resize mid-flight may wrap oddly, but content still comes through correctly.
  • One button = one fixed workflow. There's no dropdown/picker for choosing a prompt at click time; each block is one hardcoded (templated) prompt.

docs.title: Still stuck?
docs.text: Open an issue on GitHub with what you tried and what happened.

docs.title: Settings Reference
docs.text: Gear icon → Inline Agents.

docs.title: Plugin-wide
docs.text: Setting Default Default Agent Claude Code Which CLI agent note buttons run when they don't specify their own agent: line. Auto-approve by default Off When on, buttons run with permission checks bypassed unless a button sets autoApprove: false. When off, the agent asks before each tool use, right in the terminal, unless a button sets autoApprove: true. Allow JavaScript expressions in prompts Off Gates {{= expression }} segments in prompt: templates. Plain {{ file.basename }}-style lookups always work regardless of this setting — see Context and Templating.

docs.title: Per provider (Claude Code / OpenCode)
docs.text:
Setting Connection status dot green/red next to the provider name Whether the configured binary actually runs (<bin> --version exits 0) — not an auth check. Refreshed on Settings open and via the ↻ button. Binary path text field Absolute path to the executable, or a bare command name to rely on PATH. Falls back through known install locations and finally PATH lookup if the configured path doesn't exist — see Claude Code and OpenCode. Model mappings dynamic list Name → model string pairs a button's model: line resolves against — see Model Mappings.

OpenCode's model dropdown is a live list from opencode models:

docs.title: Agent runtimes
docs.text:
A second way to run a button — hand its prompt off to an HTTP agent runtime (OpenClaw, Hermes Agent, any OpenAI-compatible endpoint) instead of the inline terminal. Full detail in Agent Runtimes; summary here:

Setting Default target dropdown, Terminal plus every configured runtime name What a button without a target: line uses, and what an unknown target: name falls back to. (toggle next to it) on by default The default for a button's open: line when it's missing or malformed. Per runtime: Name, Kind (OpenClaw hook / OpenAI-compatible chat), Base URL, Agent ID or model, Token required, Send session key as x-openclaw-session-key (chat kind only), Token (masked, per-device secret storage), Thread-URL template — Add, edit or remove a runtime (no reordering — remove and re-add to change order). Two runtimes can't share a name. Test connection button, per runtime Checks reachability and the token without sending a prompt.

docs.title: Where each setting lives in the source
docs.text: For contributors: the whole tab is AgentConsoleSettingTab in src/settings.ts, using the classic imperative display() API rather than the declarative getSettingDefinitions() one — the model-mapping list (dynamically added/removed rows, a custom dropdown with a per-option copy button, live status dots) needs DOM control the declarative control types can't express. One trade-off: this tab doesn't appear in Obsidian's own in-app settings search.

docs.title: Model Mappings
docs.text: Neither CLI is told which model to use unless a button's model: line resolves to one — with no model: line at all, a button behaves exactly as it always has: no --model flag passed, the CLI picks its own default.

docs.title: Setting up a mapping
docs.text:
Settings → Inline Agents has a Model mappings list under each provider (Claude Code / OpenCode) — pairs of a short name (what you type after model: in a button) and the actual model string sent to --model. Click + to add a row, ✕ to remove one.

Each row's model field is a free-text input with a ▾ dropdown next to it listing that provider's known models:

  • Claude Code — no CLI command exists to list its models live, so this is a small curated list of the aliases/IDs claude --model --help documents (sonnet, opus, fable, haiku, and their full claude-* IDs). Type or paste any other model string directly if it's not in the list — the field never restricts you to what's in the dropdown.

  • OpenCode — a live list from opencode models, which covers every provider OpenCode is currently configured for, including a local one (e.g. an Ollama config pointed at http://host.docker.internal:11434/v1 from inside a container, or http://localhost:11434/v1 on the same machine Ollama runs on — see opencode.ai/docs/providers). Refreshed automatically when Settings opens, or on demand via the ↻ button next to the provider's name.

Every option in the dropdown has its own copy button (⧉) — use it to grab the raw model string for pasting straight into a button's model: line without setting up a mapping at all.

docs.title: How model: resolves
docs.text:
A button's model: value is resolved in this order:

  1. The name of a mapping configured in Settings for whichever agent this button ends up using (case-insensitive — myMainModel and mymainmodel both hit the same row).
  2. Failing that, the value is passed straight through as a literal model string — this is what lets you paste a raw model ID via a dropdown's copy button without configuring a mapping first.

If the key is omitted entirely, no --model flag is passed at all.

Mappings are scoped per provider

A mapping named quick under Claude Code and a button using agent: OpenCode with model: quick won't see each other — mapping names are looked up only against the agent the button actually resolves to.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: See Claude Code and OpenCode for how the agent itself is chosen.

docs.title: Claude Code and OpenCode
docs.text: Inline Agents supports two CLI agents: Claude Code and OpenCode. Neither is bundled — the plugin shells out to whichever binary you already have installed.

docs.title: Choosing an agent
docs.text:
• Per button — set agent: ClaudeCode or agent: OpenCode (case-insensitive; claude also works as a synonym for ClaudeCode) on a code block. Anything unrecognized, including the line being omitted entirely, falls back to the plugin-wide default.
  • Plugin-wide — Settings → Inline Agents → Default Agent:

docs.title: How the binary is located
docs.text:
The configured path in Settings is a preference, not a guarantee. resolveBinary() tries, in order:

  1. The path configured in Settings, if it exists on disk.
  2. A short list of known install locations for the current OS/environment (e.g. /opt/homebrew/bin/claude, ~/.local/bin/claude).
  3. The bare command name (claude / opencode), letting Node's own spawn() fall back to a normal PATH lookup.

This lets the same data.json work across different machines (e.g. a real Mac and a container) without hand-editing settings every time the vault is opened somewhere else.

docs.title: Connection status
docs.text:
Each provider's heading in Settings shows a green/red dot, refreshed automatically when Settings opens (and on demand via the ↻ button next to the provider name):

Green means the configured binary actually runs (<bin> --version exits 0); red means it doesn't (not installed, wrong path, etc.). This is a binary-resolves check, not an auth/provider-reachability check — a green dot doesn't guarantee the CLI is logged in, and a red OpenCode dot with an unreachable Ollama provider still shows as OpenCode itself being fine. Run a button to see the actual provider error.

docs.title: autoApprove and running as root
docs.text: autoApprove: true (or the plugin-wide Auto-approve by default toggle) maps to claude --dangerously-skip-permissions / opencode run --auto. Claude Code's CLI itself refuses --dangerously-skip-permissions when the process is running as root — if you're running Obsidian inside a container where it happens to run as root, auto-approved Claude Code buttons will fail with that specific error. This is a Claude Code safety restriction, not something the plugin can route around; OpenCode's --auto has no equivalent restriction.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: See Model Mappings for how to pin a button to a specific model, or Agent Runtimes for sending a button's prompt to an HTTP agent runtime (OpenClaw, Hermes Agent, any OpenAI-compatible endpoint) instead of running it here.

docs.title: Agent Runtimes
docs.text:
A button doesn't have to run in the inline terminal. target: <name> hands its rendered prompt off to an agent runtime — a named HTTP endpoint configured in Settings — so the work runs as an agent thread on that runtime and keeps going (for the OpenClaw hook kind) when the note, or Obsidian itself, is closed.

This is a second target for a button, not a replacement for the terminal: target: terminal (or no target: line at all) behaves exactly as it always has. See All Fields for target:, open: and agentId:.

docs.title: Terminal or runtime?
docs.text:
Inline terminal (target: terminal) Agent runtime (target: <name>) Where the agent runs Claude Code or OpenCode, spawned on this machine under the note An agent you already run elsewhere (OpenClaw, Hermes Agent, another OpenAI-compatible server) What you see in Obsidian A live terminal, run state, optional output written into the note A "Sent to <name>" button, optionally a link to the thread. Nothing streams back Where you read the reply In the note On the runtime (its app, chat or dashboard) Survives closing Obsidian No OpenClaw hook: yes. OpenAI-compatible chat: no Setup Install the CLI Turn on the runtime's HTTP endpoint, then add it under Agent runtimes

Use a runtime when the work belongs with an agent that has its own memory, tools and channels, and you only want the note to kick it off.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
1. Turn on the runtime's HTTP endpoint (see OpenClaw hook or OpenAI-compatible chat below).
  2. Settings → Inline Agents → Agent runtimes → add a runtime. Give it a short Name, since that's what buttons type.
  3. Paste the token and click Test connection.
  4. Add target: <name> to a button:
```agent-button
text: Hand this note to Hermes
prompt: Summarise {{file.path}} and list the open actions.
target: hermes
```
  1. Click it. The button shows "Sending to hermes…", then "Sent to hermes". Read the reply on the runtime.

docs.title: The two runtime kinds
docs.text: Kind Setting value Covers Request OpenClaw hook OpenClaw hook OpenClaw's inbound hook POST <base>/hooks/agent, asynchronous, survives Obsidian closing OpenAI-compatible chat OpenAI-compatible chat Hermes Agent, and most other OpenAI-compatible chat servers POST <base>/chat/completions, a normal user turn, runs only while Obsidian stays open

docs.title: OpenClaw hook
docs.text:
An OpenClaw instance has an inbound hook that starts (or continues) an agent session asynchronously — the run keeps going on OpenClaw's side whether or not Obsidian is still open to see it.

Example: OpenClaw is running at http://127.0.0.1:18789.

  1. In Settings → Inline Agents → Agent runtimes, add a runtime: name openclaw, kind OpenClaw hook, base URL http://127.0.0.1:18789, agent ID main, and the hook's token (e.g. <your-hook-token> — paste the real value OpenClaw gave you; the field is masked and the value never leaves this device).
  2. OpenClaw itself must have these enabled before the hook will accept a request:
    • hooks.enabled
    • allowRequestSessionKey: true
    • allowedSessionKeyPrefixes: ["inline:"] (every session key this plugin sends starts with inline: — see Session keys below)
  3. A button with target: openclaw now sends its prompt to that hook instead of running in the terminal.

OpenClaw treats the hook's text as untrusted external content, the same as any other inbound message — it does not implicitly trust it just because it came from this plugin. The request's message is prefixed with one line making clear it's an instruction from the vault owner, sent by their Inline Agents button, to reduce the chance OpenClaw summarizes it instead of carrying it out — but OpenClaw's own trust/approval policy still applies.

The run is asynchronous: once OpenClaw accepts the hook ({ ok: true, runId }), the agent keeps working there regardless of whether the note or Obsidian stays open. Closing the note doesn't stop it, and clicking the button again later starts an independent second thread.

docs.title: OpenAI-compatible chat (Hermes Agent, etc.)
docs.text: Any server exposing an OpenAI-compatible chat/completions endpoint — Hermes Agent's API server is the shipped example — can be configured as this kind.

docs.title: Example: Hermes Agent
docs.text:
Hermes Agent ships an OpenAI-compatible API server, off by default. It runs inside the Hermes gateway.

  1. Turn the API server on. Add two lines to ~/.hermes/.env (generate the key with openssl rand -hex 32):

    API_SERVER_ENABLED=true
API_SERVER_KEY=<your-generated-key>

  2. Restart the gateway with hermes gateway restart (or start it with hermes gateway). Its log should show API server listening on http://127.0.0.1:8642. Check it from a terminal:

    curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer <your-generated-key>" http://127.0.0.1:8642/v1/models

  3. Add the runtime. Settings → Inline Agents → Agent runtimes → add:

    Field Value Name hermes Kind OpenAI-compatible chat Base URL http://127.0.0.1:8642/v1 Agent ID or model hermes-agent Token required on Token the API_SERVER_KEY value Send session key as x-openclaw-session-key off (that header is for OpenClaw) Thread-URL template leave blank (see Hermes has no thread link yet)

  4. Click Test connection. It calls GET /models, so a wrong key shows up here rather than on the first click.

  5. A button with target: hermes now sends its prompt as a normal user turn (POST <base>/chat/completions, one user-role message). Nothing is prefixed onto it the way the OpenClaw hook kind's instruction line is. The turn runs on the Hermes profile whose gateway hosts the API server, with that profile's tools, memory and skills. Read the reply on the Hermes side.

The same steps work for any other OpenAI-compatible server: point Base URL at its /v1 root and set Agent ID or model to a model name it accepts.

Unlike the OpenClaw hook, this run lasts only while Obsidian stays open — there's no separate asynchronous session on the runtime's side; the request itself is the run, and a dropped connection (including Obsidian closing) cancels it. See Fire-and-forget below.

docs.title: Agent runtimes settings
docs.text:
Settings → Inline Agents → Agent runtimes:

Setting Name text, unique What a button's target: line matches against, case-insensitive. Kind dropdown OpenClaw hook or OpenAI-compatible chat. Base URL text The runtime's http(s) base URL, e.g. http://127.0.0.1:18789. No embedded credentials or query string. Agent ID or model text The OpenClaw agent id, or the chat kind's model. A button's agentId: line overrides this for that one button. Token required toggle, default on When on, a click is blocked with a notice ("token not set on this device") if no token is stored on this device, and the thread never reaches the runtime. Send session key as x-openclaw-session-key toggle, default off (chat kind only) Turn on when the chat endpoint is itself OpenClaw's, so it can see the same session key as the hook kind does. Token masked secret field Stored in Obsidian's own per-device secret storage, not data.json — see Where the token lives below. Thread-URL template text, optional Builds the link the "Sent to <name> ↗" button opens — see Thread-URL templates below. Test connection button Checks reachability and the token, without sending a prompt — see Test connection below.

Also on this screen:

  • Default target — a dropdown of Terminal plus every configured runtime name. This is what a button without a target: line uses, and what an unknown target: name falls back to.
  • The toggle next to it — the default for a button's open: line when it's missing or malformed. On by default.

Two runtimes can't share a name — the settings tab refuses to save a duplicate.

docs.title: target:, open: and agentId: on a button
docs.text:
```agent-button
text: Run weekly review
prompt: Run the weekly review on {{file.path}}
target: openclaw
```
  • target — terminal (the default) or the name of a configured runtime, case-insensitive. A name that doesn't match any configured runtime shows a notice and falls back to the Default target setting.
  • open — true/false. Defaults to the settings-wide default when the line is missing or malformed. Only matters for a runtime target: with open: true, the thread opens as soon as the hand-off settles.
  • agentId — overrides the runtime's configured agent/model for this one button only.

docs.title: What happens on click
docs.text:
1. The button shows "Sending to <name>…" and ignores further clicks until this hand-off settles — but the next click, once it has settled, starts an independent new thread (there's no "one run at a time" rule for a runtime target).
  2. The plugin picks a session key up front (see below), so it's known before the request goes out.
  3. Once settled, the button shows "Sent to <name> ↗" (a link to the thread, if the runtime has a thread-URL template) or plain "Sent to <name>" (no template configured). With open on, the thread opens at once.
  4. Every click starts a brand-new thread — there's no concept of "the same session as last time."

docs.title: Fire-and-forget, and what is not tracked
docs.text:
A runtime target is deliberately fire-and-forget:

  • No reply is streamed back into the note or the button.
  • No run state — the button doesn't track whether the agent is still working, waiting on input, or done.
  • No file output — agentOutput: file has nothing to write, because there's no captured output to write.
  • Reading the reply, continuing the thread, and any approvals all happen on the runtime itself, not in Obsidian.

Because of this, these button fields are ignored for a runtime target, with a one-line notice naming whichever ones this particular button set: model, autoApprove, agentOutput, completion, showTerminal.

Obsidian closing cancels an OpenAI-compatible chat run

The OpenAI-compatible chat kind's run lasts only as long as the request is in flight — closing Obsidian (or the note) mid-request drops the connection and cancels the run on the runtime's side. This is documented behaviour, not something the plugin handles or works around. The OpenClaw hook kind has no such limit: once accepted, it survives Obsidian closing.

docs.title: Session keys and thread URLs
docs.text: Before sending, the plugin picks a session key: inline:<note basename, URL-safe>:<epoch ms> — the note's basename lowercased, anything outside a-z 0-9 - _ replaced with -, capped at 40 characters, then the timestamp. This is why allowedSessionKeyPrefixes: ["inline:"] is what OpenClaw needs to allow.

docs.title: Thread-URL templates
docs.text:
An optional per-runtime template that builds the link the "Sent to <name> ↗" button opens, using:

Placeholder Fills in {agentId} The agent ID/model actually used for this click (the button's agentId: override, or the runtime's configured one). {sessionKey} The full session key, e.g. inline:weekly-review:1760000000000. {sessionKeyPath} The session key split on : into path segments and rejoined with / — inline/weekly-review/1760000000000.

The template can use http, https, or any custom URL scheme a runtime's own app registers — the plugin doesn't know any particular runtime's scheme, so anything is accepted except four schemes that are never safe to open automatically: file, javascript, data, vbscript. A template using one of those is rejected at settings-save time, and checked again defensively right before a thread would open.

With no thread-URL template at all, there's nothing to open — the click is fire-and-forget, the button just shows "Sent to <name>" with no link, and (with open: true) a one-time-per-runtime-per-session notice says no thread URL is set.

Opening a thread uses the operating system's own URL handler, the same way a link in any other app would — an http(s) URL opens in your default browser; a custom scheme opens whatever app registered it.

docs.title: Hermes has no thread link yet
docs.text:
Leave the Thread-URL template blank for a Hermes runtime. The Hermes desktop app can open a chat by link, but none of the placeholders above give it the right chat:

  • Hermes picks its own id for the chat a button starts, and the plugin doesn't learn it. {sessionKey} is the plugin's own key, and the chat kind only sends it as x-openclaw-session-key, which Hermes ignores.
  • The plugin's session keys contain :, which Hermes' in-app links reject.

Until that changes, a Hermes button shows "Sent to hermes" with no link, and you find the chat in Hermes yourself.

docs.title: Test connection
docs.text: Each runtime has its own Test connection button — it checks reachability and the token without sending a prompt, using whatever token is currently typed into the form (not necessarily what's already saved). For the OpenAI-compatible chat kind this calls the standard GET /models endpoint, which actually validates the token; the OpenClaw hook kind has no safe, non-prompt endpoint to check against, so this only confirms the base URL is reachable (the result message says so).

docs.title: Where the token lives
docs.text:
A runtime's token is kept in Obsidian's own secret storage, not in data.json, a note, or any log. Secret storage is per device — the token field itself is Obsidian's own masked secret-entry component, and what gets saved to data.json is only the name of the secret, never the value. If settings sync to a second device, that device has the runtime configured but has to enter the token again; until it does, a token-required runtime shows "token not set on this device" and a click falls back to the terminal rather than sending with no token.

A token never appears in a note, a thread URL, a query string, the console, a notice, or an error message — failures are reported by HTTP status and a fixed reason string only, never by echoing a header or body. "Test connection" never shows the token either.

docs.title: Falling back to the terminal
docs.text:
If anything stops the prompt from reaching the runtime, the plugin shows a notice and runs the button in the inline terminal instead — exactly as if target: had been terminal all along. Nothing here runs the prompt twice: for the OpenAI-compatible chat kind, "has the runtime accepted it yet" is decided by a 5-second rule (see below), and a fallback only ever happens before that point.

Reason Notice Fix target: names a runtime that doesn't exist Unknown target "<name>" — running the default target instead. Check the spelling against Agent runtimes in Settings, or fix the button. The runtime is unreachable (connection refused, DNS failure, or no response) <name> isn't reachable, running here Make sure the runtime's HTTP server is actually running and reachable at its configured base URL. The hook kind falls back if no response arrives within 15 seconds. The chat kind only falls back on a connection error that arrives within the first 5 seconds (see the 5-second rule below) — a chat run that is merely slow to respond is treated as sent, not unreachable. The token was rejected (401/403) token rejected Re-enter the correct token for this runtime in Settings, on this device. No token stored on this device for a runtime marked "token required" Token not set on this device for "<name>". Enter the token in Settings on this device — settings synced from another device carry the runtime's configuration but never its token. OpenClaw rejects the session key (its policy isn't enabled) OpenClaw rejected the session key: enable allowRequestSessionKey and allow the inline: prefix On the OpenClaw side, turn on allowRequestSessionKey and add "inline:" to allowedSessionKeyPrefixes.

docs.title: The chat kind's 5-second rule
docs.text:
The OpenAI-compatible chat kind has no separate "the runtime accepted this" signal of its own — there's just the HTTP response. So "settled" for this kind means 5 seconds have passed with no error:

  • An error that arrives within the first 5 seconds always falls back to the terminal — a run that fails that fast hasn't actually started on the runtime.
  • An error that arrives after the 5 seconds have already settled (the button already says "Sent", the thread may already be open) is a notice only — the terminal never runs a second copy, so the prompt is never run twice.
  • A late timeout specifically produces no notice at all, since it only means this plugin's own send stopped waiting — the run itself may well still be going on the runtime.

The OpenClaw hook kind doesn't need this: it has a real "accepted" signal ({ ok: true, runId }), so a failure before that reply is always a fallback, same as any other kind.

docs.title: What the plugin never does
docs.text:
• It never starts, installs, restarts, or configures a runtime — you turn on the runtime's own HTTP endpoint yourself, outside of Obsidian. The plugin only ever talks to a runtime you've explicitly configured, and only on a button click or "Test connection" — never on its own.
  • It makes no network request to anything you haven't configured in Agent runtimes.
  • No OAuth, no login flow, no custom header beyond a bearer token.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: See All Fields for the full agent-button field list, and Settings Reference for the rest of the settings tab.

docs.title: Your First Button
docs.text:
Open any note and drop in a fenced code block tagged agent-button:

```agent-button
text: Summarize this note
prompt: Summarize {{file.basename}} in three bullet points.
```

Switch to Reading view (or just look at it in Live Preview — it renders identically in both) and you'll see a single button:

Click it. A terminal accordion opens underneath, running whichever CLI is set as your Default Agent (see Settings Reference) with that prompt as its first message — real ANSI output, colors and all, and you can type directly into it to answer prompts or approve tool calls.

docs.title: Making it do something specific
docs.text:
Two fields are doing the work here:

  • text — the button's label.
  • prompt — what gets sent to the agent. {{file.basename}} is a context lookup — it's replaced with the current note's filename before the agent ever sees it, so the same button block works unmodified in every note you paste it into.

Everything else is optional and falls back to a sensible default — see All Fields for the complete list. A more realistic button, pinned to a specific agent and model, with its output written into the note instead of left in a terminal:

```agent-button
text: Draft this week's report
prompt: Draft a weekly report for {{file.basename}}, using the notes tagged #weekly-log from the last 7 days.
agent: ClaudeCode
model: myMainModel
agentOutput: file
append: belowButton
showTerminal: false
completion: responseEnd
```

model: myMainModel only resolves to something real once you've configured a mapping by that name in Settings — see Model Mappings. Until then it's passed straight through as a literal string, which most CLIs will reject as an unknown model — harmless while you're first wiring things up, but worth setting up before you rely on it.

docs.text:

  • Context and Templating — everything a prompt can reference, plus the opt-in expression language.
  • Examples — copy-pasteable blocks for common workflows.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: Inline Agents is a desktop-only plugin — it spawns a real CLI process (Claude Code or OpenCode) behind a PTY and needs to locate your vault on disk, neither of which is possible in Obsidian Mobile. isDesktopOnly: true in manifest.json reflects this.

docs.title: Manual install
docs.text:
1. Download main.js, manifest.json, and styles.css from the latest release.
  2. Create a folder named inline-agents inside your vault's .obsidian/plugins/ directory.
  3. Place the three downloaded files inside it.
  4. Reload Obsidian (or use Settings → Community plugins → Reload plugins).
  5. Enable Inline Agents under Settings → Community plugins.

docs.title: BRAT (Beta Reviewers Auto-update Tool)
docs.text:
If you use BRAT to track plugins directly from GitHub:

  1. Install BRAT from the Community Plugins browser if you haven't already.
  2. Run the BRAT: Add a beta plugin for testing command.
  3. Paste danrfletcher/obsidian-inline-agents.
  4. BRAT installs it and will offer updates as new releases ship.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A claude and/or opencode CLI binary installed somewhere on the machine. The plugin doesn't bundle either — it shells out to whichever you already have. See Agents and Models for how the plugin locates the binary, and each CLI's own docs (Claude Code, OpenCode) for installing it in the first place.
  • python3 on PATH (or at one of a few standard locations) — used to allocate a real PTY for the terminal. True on basically any Mac or Linux environment already.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Once it's enabled, head to Your First Button to build one from scratch.

docs.title: Completion Modes
docs.text: completion: controls when the button's spinner clears — which is a separate thing from whether the underlying agent session is still alive.

docs.title: manual (default)
docs.text:
The button stays in its loading state until the terminal session is closed, either by hand (closing the terminal, or the note itself, which sends the session SIGINT) or via the small checkmark button that appears to the right of the main button whenever a run is live under this mode. Clicking it kills the session and returns the button to idle.

This is the safest default: nothing decides "the agent is done" on your behalf.

docs.title: responseEnd
docs.text:
The button's loading state clears automatically as soon as the agent finishes responding, without killing the underlying session — it keeps running in the background until the note is closed or it's killed some other way.

This is heuristic: the plugin watches the rendered terminal for Claude Code's own turn-completion marker (a line like Crunched for 7s · done 2:54 PM) and clears the spinner when it sees one. If the agent is instead showing a dialog or question it's blocked on — a permission prompt, a "yes/no" confirmation — the spinner is swapped for a ✏️ icon instead of clearing, so a run that's actually waiting on you doesn't silently look finished.

Tuned against Claude Code, not verified against OpenCode

This detection pattern-matches text Claude Code has been observed to print. OpenCode's basic command shape is verified (see Agents and Models), but its responseEnd completion markers, dialog phrasing, or whether it uses the same conventions at all, haven't been separately checked. Treat OpenCode runs with completion: responseEnd as a test until that's confirmed.

docs.title: Example: responseEnd with a hidden terminal
docs.text:
A common pairing — run in the background, don't show the terminal, capture the result into the note once it's done:

```agent-button
text: File a follow-up (background)
prompt: Check {{file.path}} for anything marked TODO and list them.
agent: ClaudeCode
agentOutput: file
append: belowButton
showTerminal: false
completion: responseEnd
```

Clicking it shows only the button going into its loading state — no terminal pops open:

Note that with agentOutput: file, the write only happens once the process exits — not just once the turn completes. Under responseEnd the session is deliberately kept alive in the background after the spinner clears, so the file write happens later, whenever that session is eventually closed (navigating away from the note, closing it, or the vault closing). See Captured File Output.

docs.title: All Fields
docs.text:
The full agent-button shape:

```agent-button
text: Run Sufficiency Check
prompt: Run features/learning-artefacts/teacher-artefact-sufficiency-check.md on {{file.path}}
autoApprove: true
agent: ClaudeCode
model: myMainModel
agentOutput: file
append: belowButton
showTerminal: false
completion: responseEnd
```

It's deliberately a plain key: value-per-line block rather than an inline shortcode syntax — it's what Obsidian's own code-block processor is built for (works identically in Reading view and Live Preview), and it's the same shape the "Buttons" community plugin uses.

Every field except text and prompt is optional and falls back to a sensible default.

Field Values Default text any string — The button label. prompt any string — What gets sent to the agent as its first message. Supports {{ }} lookups and {{= }} expressions — see Context and Templating. autoApprove true / false plugin's Auto-approve by default setting Overrides the plugin-wide setting for this one button. When on, the agent runs with permission checks bypassed (claude --dangerously-skip-permissions / opencode run --auto). When off, it asks before each tool use, right there in the terminal. agent ClaudeCode / OpenCode (case-insensitive) plugin's Default Agent setting Overrides the plugin-wide agent choice for this one button. Unrecognized or omitted values fall back to the setting. See Agents and Models. model a mapping name, or a literal model string none (--model omitted) Which model the agent uses. See Model Mappings. agentOutput terminal / file terminal Where the agent's output ends up — see Captured File Output. append top / bottom / belowButton bottom Where the captured output gets inserted (only meaningful when agentOutput: file). showTerminal true / false true Whether the terminal accordion opens automatically on click. completion manual / responseEnd manual How the button's loading state resolves — see Completion Modes. target terminal / a configured agent runtime's name settings' Default target Where the click goes. terminal (or an unrecognised name) runs in the inline terminal as before; a runtime's name hands the prompt off over HTTP instead — see Agent Runtimes. open true / false settings' default for open Runtime targets only: whether the thread opens automatically once the hand-off settles. agentId any string the runtime's own configured agent/model Runtime targets only: overrides the runtime's agent id or model for this one button.

Example of a runtime target:

```agent-button
text: Run weekly review
prompt: Run the weekly review on {{file.path}}
target: openclaw
open: true
agentId: main
```

docs.title: {{this file}} template
docs.text: {{file.path}} in the example above is replaced with the vault-relative path of the note the button lives in — resolved from the code block's own source note (ctx.sourcePath), not whichever pane happens to be focused, so it's correct even with split panes. It's one of many available lookups; see Context and Templating for the full list.

docs.title: agentOutput: terminal vs file
docs.text:
• terminal — output stays in the live terminal accordion. Nothing is written to the note.
  • file — once the run finishes, the captured output is written into the note itself. The terminal accordion is still available while the run is live (subject to showTerminal); it's only the destination of the final result that changes. See Captured File Output.

docs.title: append positions (only with agentOutput: file)
docs.text:
• bottom — appended to the end of the note.
  • top — inserted after the frontmatter block (if any), otherwise at the very top of the note.
  • belowButton — inserted directly below the agent-button code block that triggered the run. The block's position is snapshotted at click time; if the note has changed shape by the time the run finishes (edited, block moved), the plugin sanity-checks that snapshot against the note's current content and falls back to bottom rather than risk inserting into the middle of an unrelated paragraph.

docs.title: Captured File Output
docs.text:
When agentOutput: file is set, the plugin renders the full terminal buffer to plain text once the run ends and strips out what it recognizes as its own scaffolding or CLI/TUI chrome — the $ <binary> <args> echo line, the CLI's own prompt echo, the turn-completion summary line, the persistent bottom status bar, box-drawing-only lines, and (if the session was killed mid-run) the raw Python KeyboardInterrupt traceback that PTY allocation surfaces on SIGINT.

What's left is written into the note as:

**Agent output** (<button text>, <timestamp>)

<captured content>

Real example — a button with agentOutput: file and append: belowButton, after the session behind it exited:

docs.title: What gets captured
docs.text:
This captures the whole visible session transcript (tool-call summaries included, not just the agent's final reply) rather than attempting to isolate "the assistant's message" specifically — doing real semantic extraction of just the reply would need much deeper, CLI-specific knowledge of each agent's exact output format than is safe to assume here.

It's good enough to drop into a note as a record of the run; it isn't a guarantee of a perfectly clean, chrome-free transcript in every case, especially for CLIs whose output this hasn't been tuned against.

Heuristic, not exact

Both this and completion: responseEnd work by pattern-matching the rendered terminal screen against text Claude Code has actually been observed to print, not by any structured signal from the agent itself. A CLI update that changes its output formatting, or output that doesn't match the patterns this was tuned against, can cause a stray line to survive into the captured output.

docs.title: When the write actually happens
docs.text: The write is triggered by the underlying process exiting, not by the agent finishing its reply. Under completion: manual those two things are close together (the session stays in its loading state until you close it, which is also when it exits). Under completion: responseEnd they can be far apart — the spinner clears when the agent finishes replying, but the session (and therefore the eventual file write) doesn't end until the session is later closed some other way.

docs.title: Context Reference
docs.text:
Everything a {{ }} lookup or {{= }} expression can reference, taken as a snapshot of the note the button lives in at click time — not a live handle onto the vault, so a prompt can't reach anything beyond what's listed here.

Path Value file.path Vault-relative path of the note the button is in file.basename Filename without extension file.name Filename with extension file.folder Vault-relative path of the containing folder ("" at vault root) file.extension File extension without the dot file.frontmatter.<key> Any YAML frontmatter field file.tags All tags on the note (frontmatter tags + inline #tags, deduped) file.ctime / file.mtime Creation / modification time, ISO 8601 vault.name Vault's display name vault.basePath Vault's real filesystem path date.today Today's date, YYYY-MM-DD date.now Current timestamp, ISO 8601

docs.title: Behaviour on missing or unknown paths
docs.text:
• Unknown root (e.g. {{flie.basename}}, a typo) — left in the prompt untouched, so the mistake stays visible.
  • Missing value under a known root (e.g. file.frontmatter.status when there's no status field) — renders as an empty string.

docs.title: Helper functions (inside {{= }} only)
docs.text:
Function Does join(arr, sep) Joins an array into a string with the given separator upper(s) / lower(s) Uppercase / lowercase a string default(val, fallback) val if it's set, otherwise fallback includes(collection, item) Whether an array or string contains item length(x) Length of a string or array

See Lookups and Expressions for the full expression grammar and worked examples.

docs.title: Lookups and Expressions
docs.text: prompt: isn't just a static string — it's a template rendered against a snapshot of the note the button lives in, taken at click time. Two tiers:

docs.title: {{ path.to.value }} — plain lookups, always available
docs.text:
Dot-path access into the context object. An unknown root name (e.g. a typo like {{flie.basename}}) is left in the prompt untouched, so the mistake stays visible rather than silently vanishing; a missing value under a known root (e.g. no frontmatter, or a field that isn't set) renders as an empty string.

Real example — a button using {{file.path}}, and the exact command it produced:

Notice {{file.path}} was already substituted with the note's actual path by the time the command reached the terminal — the terminal echo shows the rendered prompt, not the template.

docs.title: {{= expression }} — a small expression language, opt-in
docs.text:
For anything a plain lookup can't express — conditionals, comparisons, string building — {{= }} evaluates a compact expression against the same context, with property access (file.frontmatter.status), string/number/boolean literals, + - * / %, comparisons (== != === !== < <= > >=), && || !, a ternary (cond ? a : b), and a small fixed set of helper functions: join(arr, sep), upper(s), lower(s), default(val, fallback), includes(collection, item), length(x). For example:

prompt: {{= file.frontmatter.status === "draft" ? "Finish drafting " + file.basename : "Review " + file.basename }}

This is deliberately not arbitrary JavaScript via eval/new Function — Obsidian's own community-plugin lint (eslint-plugin-obsidianmd) flags that pattern and its config marks the rule non-suppressible, a hard constraint for anything submitted to the community plugin directory, not a style preference. The plugin ships a small hand-written parser/interpreter instead: no assignment, no loops, no access to anything outside the context object, and a fixed, closed set of callable names — there's no code-execution surface to sandbox because there's no way to reach outside the grammar. It covers the realistic "compute part of a prompt from this note's metadata" use case without that risk.

Because it can run arbitrary-ish logic (however constrained) on every click, {{= }} is off by default — a button using it does nothing until Allow JavaScript expressions in prompts is turned on in Settings → Inline Agents:

While off, a button whose prompt contains {{= }} writes a clear error to the terminal and doesn't run, rather than silently sending the literal {{= ... }} text to the agent.

docs.title: Known limitations
docs.text:
• Regex-delimited, not brace-matched. Both {{= }} and {{ }} are found with a non-greedy match up to the first }}, so an expression containing a literal }} (most plausibly a nested object/array literal) won't parse correctly. Realistic prompt-building — property access, comparisons, string concatenation, ternaries, the built-in helpers — doesn't hit this.
  • &&, ||, and ? : always evaluate both sides, unlike real JS short-circuiting. Harmless in practice — everything in the expression language is a pure, total function of its inputs (property access never throws, and the only callable functions are the fixed pure helpers), so there's no side effect an unused branch could produce — but worth knowing if you were expecting a || expensiveLookup() to skip expensiveLookup().
